finding.claim: deleteAccount calls canDelete() but discards the boolean result, so no authorization is enforced. Any caller can delete any account by id (broken access control / IDOR). closeAccount correctly uses assertCanDelete, which shows the intended pattern.
finding.source: Any authenticated user calling DELETE /accounts/{id} with an arbitrary account id.

trace.note: deleteAccount(User u, long id) is the entry point for DELETE /accounts/{id}; id is attacker-controlled
Account is looked up by the supplied id with no ownership check
canDelete(u, a) returns a boolean that is ignored, so there is no throw and no early return

finding.guards_checked: canDelete (line 10) would allow only admins or the owner, but its result is unused. There is no assertCanDelete call, no exception and no other guard on this path. No framework-level auth is visible in the repo, since this is the only file. A non-existent id gives a null Account, which canDelete would NPE on, but only if its result were used.

verdict.guard_found: canDelete (AccountService.java:9) returns a boolean that is discarded at line 22; assertCanDelete (line 13) throws but is only used in closeAccount (line 29), not deleteAccount. No other guard exists.
verdict.reason: At AccountService.java:22 the boolean result of canDelete(u, a) is discarded as a bare statement, so accounts.remove(id) at line 23 runs for any authenticated user and any id, and no other guard exists in the repo.
